entities.name: Daniel Houghton
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Daniel Houghton (1740–1791), an Irish explorer, holds a significant place in the early European efforts to penetrate the interior of West Africa, specifically in the quest to chart the elusive course of the Niger River. Sponsored by the London-based African Association, his ill-fated expedition in 1790–1791 made him one of the first Europeans to venture beyond the coastal trading posts, laying crucial groundwork for subsequent, more successful explorations. His journey, though cut short by his mysterious death, was a pivotal moment in the European Enlightenment's drive for global geographic knowledge, directly influencing the era's understanding of the 'dark continent' and its vast, uncharted territories.

Houghton departed from the Gambia River in 1790, aiming to reach the legendary city of Timbuktu and ascertain the Niger's direction. He traveled eastward through the Fula kingdom of Futa Toro and the Mandinka territories, navigating complex political landscapes and facing numerous hardships. Despite his limited resources and the inherent dangers of the journey, he managed to reach Bambuk, a gold-rich region, and sent back valuable, albeit sparse, reports on the region's geography and inhabitants. His last known communication was from the town of Simbing, near the present-day Mali-Mauritania border, before he vanished in late 1791, likely dying from disease or foul play near Nioro du Sahel.
